I walked rapidly, and before long we reached my college. Only then did I consider, with a shudder, that the being I had abandoned in my rooms might remain there, alive and moving about. I dreaded the sight of the monster, but still more dreaded Henry's seeing him. Begging my friend to wait a few minutes at the foot of the staircase, I rushed upstairs to my apartment. My hand had reached the door's lock before I recovered my presence of mind. I stopped, seized by a cold trembling. Then I flung the door wide with violence, as children do when they imagine a ghost waiting on its farther side. Nothing presented itself. I ventured timidly inside: the sitting room was empty, and the hideous visitor had departed from my bedroom too. Such good fortune seemed almost beyond belief. Once certain that my enemy had really gone, however, I clapped my hands in delight and hurried down to Clerval.

We went up together, and soon the servant brought our breakfast. But I could not govern myself. More than happiness possessed me: my skin tingled with an excessive sensitivity, and my pulse raced. I could not stay still for an instant. I sprang over chairs, struck my hands together, and burst into loud laughter. At first Clerval supposed that my extraordinary spirits arose from pleasure at his arrival. Watching more closely, however, he noticed an inexplicable wildness in my eyes. My noisy, uncontrolled laughter, empty of real mirth, both startled and alarmed him.

“My dear Victor,” he exclaimed, “for God's sake, what has happened? Don't laugh like that. How unwell you look! What can be causing this?”

“Do not question me!” I cried, covering my eyes with my hands, for I fancied that the dreaded apparition was slipping into the room. “He can tell you. Oh, save me! Save me!” Believing that the monster had caught hold of me, I fought desperately and collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What feelings must have overwhelmed him? The reunion he had looked forward to with such delight had turned so strangely bitter. Yet I saw nothing of his sorrow. I lay insensible and did not regain consciousness for a very long time.

Thus began a nervous fever that kept me confined for several months. Throughout it Henry alone attended me. I later discovered that he had considered my father's age and inability to undertake such a lengthy journey, as well as the distress my illness would cause Elizabeth. To spare them that sorrow, he concealed the seriousness of my condition.

“Attend to what I say: I have mastered the speech of despair. Every word is fixed in my memory, for I am Despair itself, a strange creature—Despair exultant and full of joy. Yet those words deceive, for though the wave is dark, it has no bitterness. We stretch ourselves down, gently bid good night, and shut our eyes; upon awakening, we are free. Come, then, linger no longer, reluctant one! See this pleasant draught! It is a benevolent spirit who calls you, no mortal maiden, and in persuasive tones—oh, if only they might persuade you!—invites you to come and drink.”

As I spoke, I kept my gaze upon his face. Its exquisite beauty, the almost heavenly compassion shining in his eyes, and his gentle yet intent expression of wonder and protest changed my overwrought feelings before he uttered a word. All the harshness of despair left me, and only the tenderest sorrow remained. His own eyes, I saw, were wet as he clasped both my hands. Seating himself beside me, he said:

“You would lead me to a sorrowful act, dearest friend. Your suffering must be profound indeed to inspire such unhappy thoughts. You desire death, yet dread it, and therefore wish me to accompany you. But I am less courageous than you; even with such company, I dare not die. Hear me, and afterward consider whether you ought to draw me into your purpose, even if despair's irresistible eloquence could make dark death so attractive that the lovely heavens appeared black beside it. I beg you to listen to someone who has cherished desperate thoughts himself and yearned impatiently for death, but who has finally trodden that phantom down and destroyed its sting. Come: since you have acted Despair toward me, I shall become Una for you and guide you unharmed from his gloomy cave. Hear me, and allow yourself to be moved by words untainted by any selfish passion.

“We cannot tell what this vast world signifies, with its curious mingling of evil and good. Yet we have been set within it and commanded to live and hope. What we should hope for I do not know; nevertheless, some good lies beyond our reach which we must pursue, and that pursuit is our earthly duty. Should misfortune confront us, we must struggle against her, thrust her aside, and keep searching for what our nature teaches us to desire. I cannot say whether the promise of future good prepares us for another existence, or whether, as laborers in God's vineyard, we are simply required to help make the path smoother for those who come after us.

Once we had watched our friend duly established in his new post, our thoughts turned toward Windsor. Its proximity to London spared our departure from Raymond and Perdita the feeling of a painful separation. We said farewell at the Protectoral Palace. It was pleasant to watch my sister adopt the spirit of the performance, as it were, and try to occupy her new position with suitable dignity. Her inward pride and outward modesty were more at odds than ever. Her shyness was genuine, springing from a fear of being insufficiently valued and a touchy awareness of the world's disregard, traits she shared with Raymond. Yet Perdita considered other people's feelings more steadily than he did. Some of her reserve came from wishing to spare those about her any feeling of inferiority, though she herself never thought of them as inferior. Birth and upbringing would have equipped Idris better for ceremonial observances. But familiarity made such things effortless for her and consequently tiresome, whereas Perdita, despite every difficulty, plainly took pleasure in her station. New thoughts occupied her too fully for our leaving to cause her much distress. She parted from us affectionately and promised an early visit, but felt no regret for the circumstances that divided us. Raymond's spirits knew no bounds. He hardly knew how to employ his newly acquired authority. His mind teemed with schemes, although he had chosen none, and he assured himself, his friends, and the world that his Protectorship would be distinguished by some deed of extraordinary glory. So we discussed them and drew our reflections as our smaller party returned to Windsor Castle. We rejoiced in our release from political agitation and welcomed our secluded life with renewed eagerness. There was no shortage of occupation. My restless energy now found its sole outlet in intellectual effort, and I discovered that sustained study was an admirable cure for the spiritual fever that idleness would certainly have brought upon me. Perdita had allowed us to bring Clara back to Windsor, and she, together with my two beautiful little children, supplied continual interest and delight.

Only Adrian's health troubled our contentment. It was visibly failing, yet no particular symptom suggested the nature of his illness, unless his unusually brilliant eyes, animated expression, and flushed cheeks gave us reason to fear consumption. He himself felt neither pain nor apprehension. He devoted himself passionately to his books and rested from his studies in the company he preferred above all others: that of his sister and me.
